evening.title: Nvidia’s journey to forge the one CPU SKU to rule them all
evening.text:
Each generation of Intel Xeons or AMD Epycs brings dozens of new SKUs: high-core count parts tuned for throughput, high-frequency ones optimized for latency, low-power chips designed for the edge, and everything in between.

But if you ask Ian Finder, who heads development of Nvidia’s datacenter CPUs, for the vast majority of use cases, all those SKUs are overkill. “There was sort of an overskewing, for many years on the other vendors side of things,” he told El Reg on the sidelines of Supercomputing 2026 this week.

Nvidia is a relative newcomer to the datacenter CPU space. The company’s first part, called Grace, launched in 2023, but didn’t see widespread deployment outside AI headnodes, high-end NICs, and a handful of standalone CPU deployments by hyperscalers like Meta.

We explored the chip in greater detail earlier this year, but the GPU slinger’s latest CPU, Vera, is a different beast. In addition to showing up as part of Nvidia’s Vera-Rubin superchips, the CPU will also be offered in standalone CPU racks, storage, and context memory systems. Just this week, Nvidia announced a new rack with 192 Vera CPUs aimed at high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, which don’t translate well to GPUs. And at least on paper, a single SKU with 88 cores clocking to 3.3 GHz powers all of them.

Historically, CPUs with different combinations of cores, clocks, I/O, and power have been used in these roles.

According to Finder, most datacenter CPUs haven’t been loaded that heavily, and as a result unloaded latency has been the optimization point. As a consequence, CPUs that rely on high core counts to boost throughput often suffer from elevated loaded latencies.

On the flip side, chipmakers can optimize for loaded latency, but this usually comes at the expense of throughput. We see this pretty clearly across AMD’s last few generations of Epycs, where it designed both space-efficient Zen-C cores that prioritize throughput and fatter frequency-optimized versions that prioritize latency.

“As more cores are up and running, your latency to memory gets higher because you have to deal with congestion on the connectivity buses,” More than Moore analyst Ian Cutress tells The Reg. “What Nvidia is saying is right. Sometimes, you do have to pick between core count and core latency.”

A balanced architecture

With Vera, Nvidia sought to thread that needle to design a balanced architecture that maintains low latencies and high throughput even when all 88 cores are loaded. This does mean making some compromises – in particular, the CPU's vector unit isn’t the beefiest. But if you’ve got GPUs capable of running vectorized code, that compromise starts to make a lot more sense – and if you’re buying Vera you almost certainly do.

“If you do a few things like that, you can actually get a part that, for the workloads people care about — knowledge agents for CI/CD, for software engineering, or databases and analytics — you can build a part that gets you the same performance per core as the frequency-optimized x86 parts at the same throughput per watt as the density-optimized parts,” Finder argued.

We should note that Nvidia isn’t unique in this line of thinking. Cloud providers have long passed on the highest core-count parts in Intel or AMD’s lineup in favor of parts they feel deliver the right mix of throughput, latency, memory bandwidth, and capacity.

The reason, in part, is that cloud providers don’t know exactly what their customers will actually be doing with those cores, and so it’s better to offer something that’s well-rounded than one that has the highest clocks or lowest latency. This same logic works pretty well for agent sandboxes.

“Nvidia is confident that it understands the market well enough that one chip will cover most use cases,” Cutress said. “You could argue that Nvidia just wants to corner that bulk market.”

Having said that, there are plenty of reasons to have multiple SKUs or product lines. Throughout much of AMD’s latest launch cycle, the House of Zen has argued its chips make for better agentic CPUs because agents aren’t one workload but many. Some may benefit from higher core counts while others may benefit from higher frequency, and AMD’s more diverse portfolio offers choice.

To that point, Vera does have one trick up its sleeve: a split personality. The processor is one of the few Arm chips that supports simultaneous multithreading (SMT), but the way it works differs wildly from what Intel would call Hyperthreading.

When enabled, SMT effectively bifurcates Vera’s Olympus cores. Eighty-eight cores turns into something that functionally looks more like 176 narrower cores. So if you need more throughput than 88 cores afford, or your workload doesn’t benefit materially from a wider core, Vera does offer some flexibility.

A broader SKU stack also helps with binning. Chip manufacturing isn’t a perfect process, and you’re going to run into defective cores from time to time. Binning allows chipmakers to sell these defective chips at a discount.

Cutress suspects that Nvidia is probably doing this for its customers and it’s just not advertising them as different SKUs the way Intel and AMD have the past few decades.

For instance, a hyperscaler might be happy to take a 72-core variant of Vera that clocks a little higher or delivers more memory bandwidth per core for the same amount of power.

But for now we have just the one, for the green lord on their green throne in the land of AI where the bots lie. ®

evening.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
evening.text:
A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. 

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, due to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than the tasks in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt the task many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential to AI systems automating research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month weeks ago, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI capabilities progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to incorporate some of these fuzzier, judgment-laden tasks that could be most relevant to AI research and development into their new suite. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about the extent to which the task is relevant for AI R&D automation. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even more so to determine what these scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into their work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”

Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees ask them to do as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original task suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising research questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck to AI R&D automation, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down. 

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the tasks most relevant to AI R&D automation. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task. 

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people to complete tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move towards open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

evening.title: China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server
evening.text:
Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses.

The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance.

In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory.

On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register.

The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time.

Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools.

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.

"Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote.

Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server.

"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server."

Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.

In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code.

Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies.

This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies.

"Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

evening.title: Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses
evening.text:
The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities.

The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor.

In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call.

Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events.

The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role."

A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense.

"Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP.

"AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified."

The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary.

The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI.

The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured.

On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera.

Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.”

Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable.

The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim.

"As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said.

The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them

However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders."

Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy.

"It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said.

"Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience."

Smart specs can't shake the hate

When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees.

"Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time.

Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces.

Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time.

Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas.

On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones.

However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning.

With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general.

A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children.

evening.title: AI boom threatens circuit board crunch to rival pandemic-era chip shortage
evening.text:
The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.

The Global Electronics Association says demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.

Its report, "The PCB Squeeze: A Wake-Up Call for Global Electronics," says AI servers need increasingly complex boards. While a typical PC board has about 12 layers of tracks, AI server boards can have 40 to 60 layers or more, and each additional layer requires more resin, copper foil, and laminate.

The supply of materials is set to be constrained through at least the first half of 2027, the report says, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028.

Programs to deliver PCBs for automotive, industrial, medical and even the defense industries are being crowded out as AI soaks up scarce capacity, it claims.

The association's North American figures show orders growing much faster than deliveries. PCB bookings rose 56.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while PCB shipments increased 13.3 percent.

Fabrication capacity is expanding, aimed at meeting the increased demand from the AI infrastructure sector, especially in Asia, where more than 90 percent of the world's boards are made. The report says that $10 billion has gone toward new PCB plants in Southeast Asia, and at least as much has been invested in China over the past three years, but the raw materials are themselves constrained.

It warns of lengthening lead times for those raw materials. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three weeks a year ago, while advanced low-loss laminates now take 14 to 18 weeks for delivery, for example.

Tightening supplies usually lead to price increases, and the report says that suppliers raised laminate costs by 30 percent in September, and that the price tag of some types of E-glass cloth for circuit boards has risen by 300 percent.

The report also puts copper prices up 37 percent over the past year. Concerns have been raised about copper supplies before, as The Register has reported multiple times.

The association compares the risk with the 2021 chip shortage, when disrupted supplies left manufacturers unable to secure even relatively mundane components.

New capacity is coming, but it is late and comes in dribs and drabs, according to the report, while AI demand just keeps on absorbing it as soon as it arrives.

The association's advice is for buyers to plan early, and to share realistic forecasts with suppliers rather than double-booking. Board makers should qualify alternative suppliers of materials such as laminate and copper foil before shortages bite, but it warns against stockpiling beyond real need, which adds to forward-buying pressure.

But it would like governments to step in, of course, by tracking board and material lead times with industry and offering tax incentives for investment in advanced PCB and substrate manufacturing equipment.

The wish list also includes state investment in research and development plus qualification of new alternative materials. It would like to see loan guarantees and grants to protect critical programs and small fabricators, structured so as to sustain new capacity if forward buying unravels and demand corrects in 2027.

"Yes, we are seeing constraint in upstream materials and have been reporting it for the past couple of quarters," said Cori Masters, senior research analyst director for Supply Chain Operations at Gartner.

"In addition, AI datacenter infrastructure build out is moving capacity support to high-layer count PCBs which increase throughput time and decreases availability of line utilization for more traditional PCB products," she told The Register. ®

evening.title: DRDO’s Hypersonic Roadmap Reveals India’s Remaining Challenges
evening.text:
India’s Hypersonic Weapons Programme is progressing beyond just technology demonstrations. The challenges faced in engineering successful hypersonic weapons go beyond just reaching speeds greater than Mach 5, with factors like propulsion longevity, thermal protection, guidance and target acquisition all playing a role in ensuring experimental designs can become successful weapons.
The DRDO Technology Foresight document outlines some of the requirements. In the Hypersonic Technologies section, they outline exactly what is going to be developed and by what laboratory, such as DRDL and RCI.
The document mentions things like ‘active cooling scramjet engines’ and ‘long endurances scramjet propulsion’. However, many of these are not unproven technologies and have progressed since the foresight report was released.
Demonstration and Long Endurance propulsion
India has previously demonstrated their capability in developing hypersonic air-breathing propulsion systems. The HSTDV successfully demonstrated sustained scramjet combustion at speeds of around Mach 6 during its flight test in September 2020. This provided the foundations for future hypersonic cruise vehicle programmes.
In a further breakthrough, DRDO conducted a successful flight test of their first long-range Hypersonic Missile on 16 th November 2024. According to the Ministry of Defence, the missile was designed to carry various payloads, with a range of over 1500km. It also performed terminal maneuvers to demonstrate its high level of accuracy.
The propulsion work has continued to progress. In April 2025, DRDL conducted a test of an active cooled subscale scramjet combustor for over 1000 seconds. Then later, a full-scale combustor was tested for over 12 minutes on the ground in January 2026. On 9 th May 2026, DRDO announced another test had been conducted for over 1200 seconds.
This test used indigenously developed liquid hydrocarbon endothermic fuels and high temperature thermal barrier coatings. These are very important as the endothermic fuels can absorb heat when they decompose.
Technology Required in the Missile
DRDO’s foresight document outlines a number of technologies required: Materials: High temperature materials for long endurance, ultra-high temperature coatings, thermal barriers, special adhesives/sealants and additive manufacturing for thermal protection.
An important point highlighted here is the Radome ablatives. The seeker in the missile needs to still receive signals and process them while the missile experiences extreme aerothermal loads. Designing a radome that can protect the missile without affecting its radio frequency.
Guidance and Control: Reaction control systems for hypersonic glide vehicles, wave rider design, compact electronically steered multifunction radio frequency systems and supersonic/hypersonic bistatic radar signal analysis.
Reaction control systems allow for maneuverability in high speed flight, wave rider design allows lift using the shockwave generated by the missile and advanced radar/radio frequency systems will allow accurate detection and tracking.
Multi domain capabilities and AI for frequency selective surfaces.
Defence aspects
India’s hypersonic capabilities raises the question of how to detect and intercept similar systems developed by potential enemies.
According to reports, DRDO’s Phase III Ballistic Missile Defence systems include specialized interceptors for maneuverable hypersonic glide vehicles and hypersonic cruise missiles. This has been referred to in defence reports as AD-AH and AD-AM.
However, details of how the programme is progressing and what dates they are aiming to conduct tests are not known. They are simply the plans for development.
It is likely that detecting these hypersonic glide vehicles will be a large issue. They can maneuver at high speeds, making it difficult for radar to track. Having space based sensors could provide early warning and tracking capabilities, however this would require significant investment into satellites, ground systems, processing and secure communication.
Progression and Longevity
India has made great progress in developing key aspects of hypersonic technology. However, these are all separate projects and do not mean that we have a fully developed operational hypersonic cruise missile/interceptor.
While reports say the long-range anti ship missile will have a range of 3500km and will be trialled and produced around 2028/29, this is a projection and not an officially confirmed production plan. While the government announced the missile would have a range of over 1500km in November 2024, there was no mention of a 3500km version or when it would be cleared for production.

evening.text:
The claim made by Pakistan, that it shot down 4 Indian Rafale aircraft in the fighting of May 2025, has been re-ignited by Chinese media ‘Sohu’. This is due to the latest FlightGlobal military aircraft directory showing 32 active Rafale aircraft within the Indian Air Force compared to the initial 36 purchased from France.
As highlighted in the article dated 20 th November, Sohu states that this equates exactly to Pakistan’s claim of 4 Rafales shot down. It criticises foreign media outlets for still describing Pakistan’s claim as “unconfirmed.”
This argument assumes that a change in active aircraft numbers equates to combat losses. However, within the FlightGlobal directory, it is unclear which 4 aircraft are ‘lost’, nor are their serials given or an explanation for the reduction in quantity. Additionally, this issue must be assessed in the context of a maintenance contract put out by the IAF in June 2026.
The contract outlines bridge support requirements for the IAF Rafale fleet, however calculations were based on all 36 aircraft being operated. The expected usage was 150 operational hours per year, so over 5 months the total hours required was 2,250.
Despite this, the fact that all 36 aircraft were immediately operational cannot be definitively confirmed. evening.title: Microsoft's last non-security preview of 2026 packs a punch
evening.text:
Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview update of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for users who prefer darker rooms.

The optional KB5132057 update arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday. Microsoft is skipping December's non-security preview because of reduced holiday operations, though that doesn't cancel the monthly security release. This last preview is quite a doozy.

The big-ticket item is the "new Windows Search Experience." We saw a preview of this last month, and Microsoft has gone well beyond the "just make it work" request of many Windows users. Results appear faster with less clutter, the tool uses memory better, and files can be previewed directly in Windows Search.

We're less convinced by inline actions, which let users perform common tasks directly through Windows Search without opening Settings. In our testing, "turn on dark mode" worked, but "switch on dark mode" did not, thus highlighting the limitations of the tool. In addition, we remain unconvinced that Windows Search is the place to run actions.

That said, anything that makes Windows Search less of a punchline for unkind jokes about performance and accuracy is welcome, as are other features, including an optional screen-brightening feature for Windows Hello facial recognition in dim rooms, and the PowerToys-esque Run dialog, which users can enable in Settings.

While some of the new features won't be enabled immediately, Microsoft has included fixes that will be available right away. One addresses an issue where Windows Fax and Scan could fail to connect to a fax server. Handy for those occasions when email falls over into a heap.

There are also fixes for Windows IoT Enterprise LTSC activation failures and the misleading "Something went wrong" message shown on Android devices during cross-device passkey authentication. At the time of writing, Microsoft still lists the problem as something for which "we are working on a resolution to be released in a future Windows update."

Sadly, not everything has been pushed off the naughty step. SQL Server queries using OLE DB providers can still leave connections to external databases open after they've finished. Microsoft is working on that one and "will provide an update in an upcoming release." ®

evening.title: Microsoft suggests Registry hack to work around hotpatch woes
evening.text:
Some Windows 11 applications might fail to install or launch after Microsoft's November hotpatch, but not to worry: there's a Registry tweak to work around it.

Microsoft has confirmed it isn't administrators' imaginations. The November hotpatch is causing application errors, including in little-used and obscure apps such as Outlook.

Affected applications may fail during installation, launch, or use, displaying errors such as "ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099)." Microsoft's investigation points to applications that load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, msi.dll. The problem is more common with 32-bit software, but can also affect 64-bit applications "under certain circumstances."

The workaround involves fiddling with the Registry on affected devices, so is not for the faint of heart and a backup is a good idea before diving in. Microsoft says the key "HotPatchTableSize" in the folder "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management" needs to be set to "2000" followed by a restart.

Just the thing to round out the week for administrators.

The issue affects the November hotpatch, not the standard monthly cumulative security update. "Devices which installed the November 2026 Windows monthly security update are not expected to be affected by this issue," Microsoft said.

Windows hotpatches are security updates that don't require a device restart (unless, as in this instance, administrators have to do so to address errors after a hotpatch is installed). Windows 11 hotpatching requires version 24H2 or later, an eligible subscription, and the necessary management and security configuration.

"Hotpatch update package size is significantly smaller than the standard cumulative updates," Microsoft said, and the goal is to "streamline the installation process and enhance compliance efficiency."

The offending hotpatch, KB5132043, was released on November 10. It followed the October 13 baseline, which was a prerequisite.

Microsoft made hotpatching the default in Windows Autopatch earlier this year. At the time, we asked: "What could possibly go wrong?"

Thanks to November's hotpatch, we have our answer. ®

evening.text:
India’s defence industrial cooperation with Japan may take a significant step forward with reports that Japan has proposed licensing the production of enhanced variants of the Mogami-class Multi-role Frigate at Indian shipbuilding facilities. This follows increased cooperation between the nations in naval technologies, including the installation of a UNICORN integrated mast system on the Mogami Class.
On 18 th November, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh visited the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF) base at Yokosuka to tour the JS Natori Mogami-class frigate with his Japanese counterpart Shinjiro Koizumi.
According to Bharat Shakti, Japan has proposed that India locally produce an enhanced variant of this frigate with technology transfer. Pricing, production, technology transfer and requirements from the Indian Navy are currently being discussed. The proposal may see production within shipyards in India such as Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited (MDL) or Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers (GRSE).
However, no official confirmation has been given by either the Indian or Japanese governments, meaning that this proposal is still under discussion.
UNICORN
This proposal builds on an existing partnership between India and Japan regarding UNICORN integration masts.
In November 2024, India and Japan signed a Memorandum of Implementation for collaboration on developing the Unified Complex Radio Antenna (UNICORN) system for installation on Indian Navy vessels. The deal was signed between India’s Ambassador to Japan and the Commissioner of Japan’s Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency (ATLA).
The system combines various radio communication devices, reducing numbers of antennas on board. Due to its compact design, and radome with a low radar cross section, the system is designed to increase stealth capabilities.
The UNICORN system (or NORA-50) was developed by a joint partnership between NEC Corporation, Sampa Kogyo and Yokohama Rubber. It is installed on the Japanese JMSDF Mogami class frigates.
Through this collaboration, key development and production will be led by Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) in India with technology support from Japan. The agreement signed in November 2024 marks the first collaborative development and production of defensive equipment between India and Japan. In India, this licensing production would allow for the transfer of Japanese ship design and production technologies, as well as local shipyards participating in production. As part of this proposal, Indian weapons systems may be incorporated, with possible inclusion of BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles. Final configurations will depend upon discussions and requirements of the Indian Navy. However, the timing of the visit is notable as on 19 th November, India and Japan held their 4 th Foreign and Defence Ministers’ 2+2 dialogue in Tokyo. During this meeting, defence industrial cooperation and maritime security between the two nations was discussed.
After the meeting, Singh stressed that agreements should be made as soon as possible regarding the UNICORN naval mast project. Additionally, Singh discussed the wider vision for cooperation between the two countries, “Design with Japan, Make in India”. Both nations aim to increase cooperation in niche areas of defence technologies, such as underwater and missile technologies.
Both nations also discussed cooperation in maritime and aerial domain awareness, Search and Rescue efforts, data sharing, mutual access to ship repair facilities, and mine detection capabilities.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal

To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars.

In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it.

  • Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever.
  • AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?”
  • Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.”
  • It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.”
  • There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.”

To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand.

evening.title: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand
evening.text:
The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.

The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.

The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government.

The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters.

The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month.

A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers.

For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected.

While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.

At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens.

In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US.

Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators.

Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless.

Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not.

What the judgment does not confirm

While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public.

"Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest.

"We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed.

"That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now."

The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026.

The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users.

The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals.

A government spokesperson said: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public.

"A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data.

"Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

"Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies."

Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

evening.text:
TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption.

The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

evening.title: Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in
evening.text:
A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again."

Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored."

Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.

Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.

An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

evening.title: Ubuntu Core Desktop targets 28.04 debut, with default status in its sights
evening.text:
Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04.

Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. Yes, we know, we have heard this before: we reported on his plans last month. But this time, there's the beginning of a release schedule.

Seager said that Ubuntu Core is already out there in tens of thousands of IoT devices – which seems like a modest estimate to us, and to him too, as he quickly added "maybe more." Despite some noise a few years ago, though, what's still missing is the desktop version.

Seager's slides listed three bullet points: that Core Desktop will be "immutable," "composable," and "attestable."

As he put it, they are "taking the whole of the Linux operating system, and cramming the whole thing into snaps." Acknowledging that this is going to be wildly controversial, he said: "This is one for the Redditors."

He's right. There is a lot of resistance to snap, and in direct response, advocacy of the Red Hat-backed Flatpak instead – but we have seen almost none that is based on either system's technical merits. Much of that opposition concerns claims of one being more open than the other. We've looked at how both systems work, and our impression is that the implementation of snap is cleaner, simpler, easier to use, and more comprehensible. Snap does depend on systemd, which Flatpak does not – but only for now. Flatpak NG is in development and will also need everyone's favorite init system.

Ubuntu Core's immutability is not new technology: even Core 16 is now a decade old. It has supported in-place version upgrades since Core 22.

We have reported before that Canonical remains strongly committed to its packaging format, and that commitment seems stronger than ever. Seager continued: "Never has a model like snap confinement been more relevant… we're finally in a position where we can bring this to the desktop."

The core idea of an immutable OS is that "much more of the system is not writable at runtime," meaning that it "can't be messed with once the system has booted." He talked about the same three use cases we discussed last month. The "browser-centric machine" is the company's analog to Google ChromeOS, and he said that it's essentially ready now, suggesting that everyone listening probably has a family member whose computer is basically just a way to use a web browser.

The second was the dedicated games machine, which we interpret as a response to Valve's SteamOS. This edition, he said, would "boot straight to Steam," with "just enough of a shell to launch games." There's also an immutable "development workstation," and here, he offered the example of developers who need to work on some long-unsupported hardware or software, for whom an immutable OS means that you "can't brick your system by installing some weird old dependencies, unmaintained for 20 years."

Another important benefit is "atomic, transactional updates," which he said "brings enormous stability." The terminology comes from the database world: an atomic operation succeeds as a whole or is not applied. The aim is to avoid leaving the system stranded between incompatible package versions, with rollback providing a route back if an update causes trouble.

The "composable" part means assembling the OS from separately packaged components, from desktop environments to underlying services such as PipeWire and fingerprint-reader support.

Here, Seager used an example that spoke to us. He asked: "Ever installed something and watch as it spewed stuff all over your system?" Yes, we have, many, many times. You install one innocent-seeming little component, and it brings in a database, three new server components, and about half of a different desktop environment. We mentioned an example when we described how to customize Xfce a couple of months ago. That time around, in Debian, we found it was safe to install all packages starting with "xfce4-" except "xfce4-dev-tools." Most are tiny panel controls taking just hundreds of kilobytes, but the "dev-tools" package also pulls in several hundred megabytes of compilers, linkers, and other programming tools, totally unrelated to desktop layouts – and once installed, they're surprisingly tricky to remove again.

This is part of the appeal of a composable immutable OS: adding a component need not mean tangling its dependencies into the base system. But easier housekeeping isn't the only attraction. Canonical kept snap packages from its cancelled phone and tablet OS because snaps enable it to maintain a single package of, for instance, Firefox, which will work on all of its different OS versions that are still getting updates. Moving such important external dependencies into isolated snap packages makes it easier and safer to upgrade from one version of the OS to another. Complex sets of dependencies are the main point of failure of OS upgrades, especially when the OS has been used for a while.

This is very much not a solved problem. For instance, Debian version upgrades can be fraught – especially when the installation has decades of history behind it. Debian does at least support version-to-version upgrades. For many years and versions, RHEL did not – which is why we highlighted AlmaLinux's tooling for the task. Zorin OS added version-to-version upgrades in 16.3 just a few years ago. Linux Mint introduced its own upgrade tooling a few years earlier, although it still imposes restrictions.

It's a tough issue to crack. Major enterprise vendors discourage it, and phone OSes are all immutable. Helping with this problem is one of the main reasons snap packaging exists, while Flatpak is almost entirely irrelevant to it.

Seager also stated that Core Desktop would support "multiple desktops from the start." This will not be a GNOME-only project. Indeed, he specifically mentioned a KDE Plasma version, saying: "Plasma is great. People love it. We will have a KDE edition, with rolling Plasma. We will deliver upstream Plasma, as fast as we can." That sounds like a very welcome counterpoint to the LTS version of Plasma 6.6 in Kubuntu 26.04 whose announcement we covered back in August.

For the "attestable" line of the slide, he claimed that Core Desktop was "evolving the way we think about 'trust' on a machine. We have TPM, secure boot, TPM-backed Full Disk Encryption… but they're all bolt-ons." Core Desktop, he added, could "tie this into a hardware root of trust," delivering "verified system integrity." Canonical revived its TPM-backed full-disk encryption system back in 2025, and it arrived in Ubuntu 26.04. Back in January, systemd creator Lennart Poettering launched his startup Amutable, and earlier this month published a technical overview of its new immutable Linux. We suspect Canonical is watching closely, and that this is a hint in that direction.

We were also amused by Seager's mention of another rather niche distro: he said that Core Desktop would deliver "all of the joy that people derive from NixOS, for those with that perverse habit – but for everybody."

Daily preview installation images of Core Desktop will, apparently, be available very soon, in both GNOME and KDE flavors, and he warned that "there be dragons." (That may be a veiled nod to one of founder Mark Shuttleworth's other companies.)

After the promises made in 2023, we'll be watching that timetable closely. "I believe this is the future of Linux," Seager said, promising "a final version by 28.04, released alongside Ubuntu," adding that a "very stretchy stretch goal was by default for 30.04: download from ubuntu.com and you get Core Desktop – unless you ask for the other thing."

For those alarmed by that prospect, he had reassurance: "Ubuntu as you know it today is not going anywhere. There are no plans for the existing distro to go away."

Core Desktop wasn't even the main subject of his keynote. They followed a lengthy excursion into formal logic: definitions, proofs, invariants, and designing software whose behavior can be checked against precisely stated rules. The accompanying slides showed the logos of organizations working in this area, such as Hegel, Antithesis, and the Lean programming language. For now, an entire OS is much too big to formally verify, but subcomponents may be doable – and Canonical is starting with snapd.

He also expressed his satisfaction with the Stonking release, highlighting that it advanced Canonical's move toward Rust-based components, including Rustls and upki – noting that this proved very timely in the light of recent events. The release also delivered the newest available kernel, OpenSSL 4 – which he called a "huge change" – and official RISC-V images. He also called out the Myna speech-recognition feature, saying that it was all in-house, designed and shipped in six months by a team of "about two and a half people." It will form part of the company's plans for what it calls a context-aware desktop. ®

evening.title: Support tech fixed malware by charging client less for their services
evening.text:
Welcome to Friday and therefore to another edition of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed tech support column in which we share your tales of cleaning up messes made by clients and colleagues.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Dennis" who told us he once ran a tech support business in a major US city.

"I got a call from a very well-known lawyer's office," he told On Call. "Over the two decades I spent supporting his office, this attorney and I became close friends."

The attorney was also a good client because Dennis found himself billing a three-figure sum every month for malware removal that resulted from the lawyer’s – ahem – personal browsing habits.

Dennis eventually tired of malware removal and told his client to expect a substantial bill for the iMac he was about to buy as a replacement for his PC.

"I told him this would pay for itself in 18 months," Dennis wrote, because he figured it wouldn't get malware all the time.

"He actually said, with genuine concern: 'If you do that, you will make less money'."

Dennis replied that he aimed to give his clients the best advice, and that on this occasion his counsel was to pay Apple instead of himself!

"It took him about five years to stumble across anything that could harm that iMac," Dennis wrote. "When he did, I had no idea what to do: I had never seen an infected Apple product."

So he did what all tech support people do: reinstalled the OS and crossed his fingers.

Dennis was rewarded when the machine came back to life, with all data and settings intact.

"I had given up at least $6,000 in support revenue by solving his problem and I'd do it again," he wrote, before winding up his story by letting us know "I retired five years ago. It’s still on his desk!"

Have you done less tech support to deliver more value? If so, click here to send On Call an email and charge us with the responsibility of telling your story on a future Friday. ®
